prompt: Which of these is an observation rather than a judgement?
hint: What would a camera have recorded?

choices.text: “You’re not a team player, and the rest of the team has started to notice it too.”
choices.why: A judgement about who the person is, with a claim about others attached.

choices.text: “You need to communicate more with the team.”
choices.why: A conclusion with no instruction about what “more” looks like.

choices.text: “Your code is sloppy.”
choices.why: An adjective about the work, with nothing a camera would show.

choices.text: “You declined the last three requests to pair.”
choices.why: Right: it is something that happened and could be checked.

prompt: Why do people defend against a judgement harder than against an observation?

choices.text: Judgements are usually wrong
choices.why: They may be right; the problem is that they are arguable and about identity.

choices.text: Observations are always delivered more gently
choices.why: Delivery is a separate matter; an observation can be said harshly too.

choices.text: People do not listen to managers
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson suggests this.

choices.text: A judgement is about what they are, and nobody knows how to change what they are, while what they did can be done differently next time
choices.why: Right: identity is defended harder than action, because action can change and identity cannot be changed on request.

prompt: Renata has an impression that somebody is “disengaged” but cannot find a specific moment behind it. What does the lesson say she has?

choices.text: Feedback to give at once, before it gets worse
choices.why: Without a moment the person could picture, it would be a judgement.

choices.text: An impression to watch for and note privately
choices.why: Right: without observations there is no feedback yet, only something to watch and write down.

choices.text: Grounds for a performance conversation
choices.why: A performance conversation needs far more than an impression; lesson 10 covers it.

choices.text: Nothing worth keeping
choices.why: It is worth keeping, in the private notes, until there is something concrete.

prompt: Match each judgement with its observation from the lesson’s table.

pairs.right: four of six proposals met with “that won’t work”
two pull requests without error-path tests came back from review
the slip reached Renata through Helena, not through you
the runbook let Thiago fix the alert alone at 3 a.m.

right_distractors: you have a bad attitude about reviews

prompt: Put the parts of the Center for Creative Leadership’s feedback structure in order.
hint: When, what, and what it caused.

prompt: Which sentence is the impact in Renata’s feedback to Diego?

choices.text: “Your first comment was ‘this is wrong, redo it’, and it didn’t say what was wrong.”
choices.why: That is the behaviour, what a camera would record.

choices.text: “Thiago didn’t push anything for two days.”
choices.why: Right: an observable effect of the comment.

choices.text: “The review on Thiago’s pull request on Tuesday.”
choices.why: That is the situation.

choices.text: “You were too harsh with him.”
choices.why: A judgement, and not in Renata’s feedback at all.

prompt: Why did Renata end the impact with Thiago going to Yara for reviews?

choices.text: To make Diego jealous of Yara
choices.why: Nothing in it is about rivalry.

choices.text: Because Yara had complained about the extra reviews landing on her desk every week
choices.why: Yara had not complained; the point was the calendar code.

choices.text: To show the team had sided with Thiago
choices.why: It describes one effect, not a team taking sides.

choices.text: It tied the behaviour to something Diego himself cares about, which is the quality of the calendar code
choices.why: Right: the person who knows the calendar code best was no longer reviewing it.

prompt: Which of these does situation-behaviour-impact leave out on purpose? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look at the line under the figure.

choices.text: Comparisons with how other people do it
choices.why: Yes: Renata said nothing about how others review.

choices.text: The effect the behaviour had
choices.why: No: the impact is one of the three parts.

choices.text: Adjectives about the person
choices.why: Yes: no “harsh”, no “arrogant”.

choices.text: The day it happened
choices.why: No: the situation anchors it in a specific moment.

choices.text: Guesses about what the person intended
choices.why: Yes: intent is the person’s to tell, not the manager’s to assume.

prompt: What did Renata learn by asking Diego how the review went, before giving the feedback?

choices.text: That Thiago had asked for blunt comments
choices.why: That was a hypothetical in the lesson, to show how an answer could change the feedback.

choices.text: Nothing she did not already know
choices.why: She learned that he regretted it and did not know about the two lost days.

choices.text: A lapse, not a style
choices.why: Right: her feedback could be shorter, and Diego named the problem himself.

choices.text: That Diego thought Thiago’s pull request was badly written and deserved the comment
choices.why: He said the comment was short because he wrote it between meetings, not that it was deserved.

prompt: When does asking first become a trap?
hint: Could the answer change what you say?

choices.text: When nothing could change it
choices.why: Right: then the question only waits for a confession, and people recognise it.

choices.text: When the person is senior
choices.why: Seniority does not make the question a trap.

choices.text: When the feedback is positive
choices.why: The lesson does not discuss this case as a trap.

choices.text: When the manager has not prepared the situation, behaviour and impact in writing beforehand
choices.why: Preparation is not what makes it a trap; a closed mind is.

prompt: Match each of Kim Scott’s quadrants with what it does.

pairs.right: cares about the person and challenges the work
cares, and never says the hard thing

prompt: An engineer made a joke about a colleague’s accent in a team meeting. Should the manager open the conversation with “How do you think that meeting went?”

choices.text: Yes: asking first always works better
choices.why: The lesson names exactly this kind of case as the exception.

choices.text: Yes, so that he can explain the joke and the manager can judge whether it was really meant to offend anybody
choices.why: Intent does not change what the joke did, and the lesson puts serious cases outside asking first.

choices.text: No: the manager should raise it in the next team meeting instead
choices.why: Corrective feedback is private, and this is a conversation with him first.

choices.text: No: for serious behaviour, say what happened and what it means first
choices.why: Right: asking first would make discriminatory behaviour sound negotiable.

prompt: What does the lesson say should be in a performance review that the person has not heard before?
hint: A summary of conversations that took place.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right: everything in it should already have been said, close to when it happened.

choices.text: The corrective feedback, saved for the formal moment
choices.why: Saving it is what the lesson argues against.

choices.text: The rating, which managers decide only at review time and should not hint at before
choices.why: A rating may be decided then, but the feedback behind it should not be new.

choices.text: Praise from colleagues
choices.why: Nothing says praise should be held back for the review.

prompt: Why does the lesson say “say it first, write it after”?

choices.text: Written feedback is not legally valid
choices.why: Nothing legal is involved.

choices.text: Because writing takes longer
choices.why: Writing is often quicker, which is why it is tempting.

choices.text: In writing the person cannot ask what you meant, and you cannot see how it lands
choices.why: Right: and a sentence gentle out loud reads cold on a screen; the written version is the record afterwards.

choices.text: People do not read messages
choices.why: They read them; what is lost is the conversation.

prompt: A manager writes in the team channel after an incident: “Whoever deployed on Friday without checking the dashboard, please don’t.” Which rules from this lesson does that break?
hint: Where, how, and what it describes.

choices.text: None: it names no one, so it is private
choices.why: Everybody on the team knows who deployed on Friday.

choices.text: Only the timing, since it should have waited for the review
choices.why: Waiting for the review would break another rule; soon was right, the place and form were wrong.

choices.text: It is a judgement rather than an observation
choices.why: It describes a behaviour; the problems are where and how it was said.

choices.text: Corrective feedback given in public, in writing first, with no conversation
choices.why: Right: it is public, written, and leaves the person no chance to explain or ask.
